summary:
Dust Shift: Survive the Lunar Dust is a retro pixel-art survival game that runs in the browser. You command Outpost Halo, a four-person Moon base at the lunar south pole, and have 14 days to keep the crew alive until the relief ship arrives. Each day brings a new event, and you pick one response. Every choice helps one resource and costs another, so you’re constantly balancing power, air, suit seals, and crew health against the creeping buildup of sharp, sticky lunar dust.

It has three difficulty levels (Rookie, Astronaut, Legend), a 3-day tutorial, and a story told through the crew’s daily log, including a recurring thread about Tomas and his daughter’s drawing. Runs end with a rank and score out of 100, and there are nine different endings to discover. A “Was that real?” section at the end links the gameplay to real lunar dust science from the Apollo missions and current engineering work on seals, coatings, and dust shields.
details:
What it does and how it works

Dust Shift is a browser-based survival game set at Outpost Halo, a four-person base at the lunar south pole. Players have 14 days to keep the crew alive until the relief ship arrives. Each day brings one event, such as dust-caked solar panels, a moonquake, a solar flare alert, or a decision about how to split a tank of water ice. The player picks one of several responses. Every choice moves five meters (power, oxygen, suit seals, crew health, and dust), helping one and costing another. Dust rises every day, and when it gets high it wears out seals and leaks air, so cleaning always costs power or crew energy.

Events are shuffled, so every run plays differently. Each run ends with a score out of 100, a rank (Cadet, Bronze, Silver, or Gold), and one of nine story endings. There are three difficulty levels (Rookie, Astronaut, Legend) and a 3-day tutorial led by Commander Mira. A “Was that real?” section then links the gameplay to real lunar dust science.

Benefits

  • It makes a real engineering problem understandable to people with no technical background.
  • It needs no install or account, and it works on phones and desktops, in light or dark mode.
  • Short, replayable sessions make it easy to use in a classroom or at an outreach event.
  • Because every option has a cost, players practice trade-off thinking instead of looking for one right answer.

Intended impact

We want players, especially students and space fans, to understand why lunar dust is one of the hardest problems for future Moon bases. We also want them to see that real mission planning is about balancing competing needs, and to care about the people on the crew.

Tools, languages, and hardware

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks or build step. The whole game is one self-contained file.
  • Graphics: an inline SVG pixel-art scene that changes across four story phases (Settling In, Dust Storm Season, The Long Night, Dawn of the Relief Ship).
  • Audio: the Web Audio API generates every sound effect and the ambient soundtrack, so there are no audio files. Players can toggle sound on or off.
  • Storage: the browser’s localStorage saves run history and unlocked endings.
  • Fonts: Google Fonts (Press Start 2P and VT323).
  • Hardware: no special hardware. Any device with a modern web browser works.
  • Team tools: [add your code editor, hosting service, and any other software]

How it’s creative

  • It turns a technical hazard into a story. The crew has names and personalities, and a recurring thread follows Tomas and the drawing his daughter Lia made for him.
  • Every choice has a cost, and each result comes with a short, witty line, so the game stays light even while teaching hard lessons.
  • The retro pixel-art look and fully synthesized soundtrack give it a handmade arcade feel.
  • Real science is built into the gameplay rather than added as a lecture afterward.
